did_you_know.text: Did you know? The seventh month in the biblical calendar is our current month of Tishrei, and it marks the beginning of the civil year in Judaism.
Did you know? 'Yom Teruah' (Day of Shouting/Blowing) is a unique name for Rosh Hashanah, emphasizing the commandment to sound the shofar and its distinctive blast.
Did you know? Already on Rosh Hashanah, the Day of Judgment, a sin offering is brought – which teaches about the need for introspection and repentance at the beginning of the year.
Did you know? The commandment 'afflict your souls' on Yom Kippur is interpreted as five forms of affliction: fasting, refraining from washing, anointing, wearing leather shoes, and marital relations.
Did you know? The 'sin offering of atonement' mentioned here refers to the special goat sent to Azazel or offered inside the Holy of Holies, as detailed in the Book of Leviticus.
Did you know? The word 'Chag' (feast) in this context often refers to festivals that include the commandment of pilgrimage to the Temple in Jerusalem, such as Sukkot.
Did you know? The festival of Sukkot begins with the largest number of bull offerings – thirteen – a number that decreases daily throughout the seven days of the festival.
Did you know? Unique to the festival of Sukkot is the number of bulls that decreases daily, from 13 on the first day to 7 on the seventh day.
Did you know? A total of 70 bulls were offered throughout the entire Sukkot festival, a number traditionally symbolizing the seventy nations of the world for whom prayers are offered on the holiday.
Did you know? 'Atzeret' is a separate holiday from the seven days of Sukkot, also known as 'Shemini Atzeret,' and it signifies a more intimate and personal day with God.
Did you know? On Shemini Atzeret, the number of sacrifices dramatically decreases (only one bull and one ram), emphasizing the unique and more intimate nature of the day compared to Sukkot.
Did you know? The Torah distinguishes between obligatory sacrifices, like those for the festivals, and 'your vows and freewill offerings' – sacrifices that a person brings of their own accord.
Did you know? The phrase 'pleasing aroma' does not describe a physical scent, but rather expresses the good will and intention of the offerer, which are accepted and desired before God.
